blocks.h2: What to Do If You Smell Gas
blocks.intro: A gas smell is one situation where waiting is not an option.

steps.body: Don't stop to grab belongings, and don't switch any lights or electronics on or off.
Once you're outside, call your gas utility or 911 to report it. Don't go back in until the area has been cleared.
Once it's safe, call a licensed plumber to locate and fix the source. We'll find it and repair it.

blocks.h2: Warning Signs of a Gas Line Problem
blocks.intro: Corrosion is slow. But when it catches up, these are some of the signs:

tiles.h3: A Rotten Egg or Sulfur Smell
tiles.body: Even a faint smell of rotten eggs indoors is worth taking seriously.
A hissing sound near a gas line or appliance can mean gas escaping from a fitting or pipe.
Dead or discolored grass above a buried gas line can point to a leak underground.
A gas bill that's higher than normal with no change in usage can mean gas is going somewhere it shouldn't.

bodies: Finding the leak is the first step of every gas line repair. We locate leaks with pressure testing and gas detection equipment, checking the line from the meter to each appliance, including fittings, valves and connectors that are easy to miss.

If you've noticed a faint smell, a higher bill or a hissing sound but can't find the source, a leak check tells you what's going on before it turns into an emergency. If the smell is strong, leave first and call your gas utility or 911 from outside.

blocks.h2: Gas Line Problems in Highland Park Homes
blocks.intro: The median Highland Park home was built in 1963, and about 1 in 4 went up before 1940. Gas piping ages along with the house.

items.body: Many older homes still run on original black iron or steel gas piping. Corroded fittings and old valves fail slowly, and a leak can go unnoticed for a long time.

A single failed fitting is a repair. When the pressure test and inspection show widespread corrosion, replacing the run can save you from chasing one leak after another. We'll explain both before you decide.

blocks.h2: Gas Line Questions From Highland Park Homeowners

items.q: How do you find a gas leak?
items.preview: With pressure testing and gas detection equipment, from the meter to each appliance.
items.answer: We use pressure testing and gas detection equipment to check the line from the meter to each appliance, including fittings, valves and flexible connectors. See [gas leak detection](#gas-leak-detection).

items.q: How long does gas line repair take?
items.preview: Simple repairs often take a few hours. Replacing a run can take a day or more.
items.answer: Straightforward repairs can often be completed in a few hours. Replacing a run of piping may take a full day or longer. Your technician will give you a realistic timeline after assessing the job, before any work begins.

items.q: Can I repair a gas line myself?
items.preview: No. Gas line work should be done by a licensed pro.
items.answer: Gas line work should be done by a licensed pro. Gas line repairs require specific diagnostic tools, knowledge of local code and a verification process that isn't available to unlicensed individuals.

items.q: How is gas line repair priced?
items.preview: A licensed technician assesses the job and gives you a flat rate before anything starts.
items.answer: We don't price gas line jobs over the phone. A licensed technician assesses the situation and gives you a flat rate before anything starts. That number doesn't change once you've agreed to it. If the scope changes after work begins, we discuss it with you before proceeding.
